paragraphs: When a city narrows a traffic lane to install a protected bicycle path, shopkeepers on the street often protest. Their fear is easy to understand: fewer parking spaces and slower car traffic seem to promise fewer customers. Merchants tend to estimate that most of their patrons arrive by car.

Studies conducted after such installations, however, have frequently found that sales on the affected street held steady or rose. Part of the explanation is that people who arrive on foot or by bicycle visit more often, even if each visit is small. But the shopkeepers' estimate may also be mistaken at the outset; surveys that count actual arrivals often show that drivers make up a minority of customers. For this reason, the dispute should be approached less as a clash of interests than as a question that counting can answer.
